title: Converting Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

findings.finding: The unscaffolded conversion of 5 2/3 is repeated unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both tasks request the same conversion with identical values, givens and support.
findings.checked: Compared the complete tasks and their group instructions. Neither has a diagram or a stated instructional purpose for repeating this numerical case.
findings.assumptions: No additional teacher-specified retrieval purpose is supplied.

repair.proposal: Change p14-q1-g to 5 1/3 under its existing instruction. Answer: 16/3.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy uses different values while retaining the conversion task.

findings.finding: Recurring-decimal practice requires identifying and marking repeating blocks and non-repeating prefixes before those notation decisions are taught.
findings.breakdown: Students may include a non-repeating prefix in the recurrence mark, omit a zero belonging to the cycle, or copy a rounded calculator digit.
findings.checked: Searched all preceding teaching. p18-common-fdp supplies a dotted single-digit benchmark; p20-information supplies an ellipsis example. Neither explains recurrence marks. p27-q1-c later addresses calculator rounding, but does not teach multi-digit blocks or prefixes and comes after p25-q8.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary calculator division is available; calculator use is explicit in p25-q8.

repair.proposal: Before p25-q8, add: 'Divide the numerator by the denominator. A recurring decimal repeats a digit or block forever. A dot marks a single repeating digit; a bar covers the whole repeating block, including any zeroes. Leave initial non-repeating digits outside the mark. Calculator displays are finite and may round their last digit.' Model 1/6 = 0.166666… = 0.1\dot{6}, 2/11 = 0.181818… = 0.\overline{18}, and 1/99 = 0.010101… = 0.\overline{01}, identifying each prefix and cycle.

findings.doneWhen: The notation decisions are explicitly modelled before their first independent use; the later topic can reuse that teaching.

findings.finding: Reverse conversion introduces non-recurring prefixes without supplying a method for handling them.
findings.breakdown: The preceding patterns place wholly repeating blocks over 9, 99 or 999. Applying those patterns unchanged to 0.0\dot{4} produces 4/9 or 4/99 instead of 2/45; a nonzero prefix also requires combining separate contributions.
findings.checked: p28-q3–q5 teach wholly recurring conversions through explicit patterns. Earlier place-value teaching handles terminating decimals, and earlier fraction-to-decimal questions do not model this reverse decision. The mastery label does not supply the missing method.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary fraction operations and decimal scaling are prior knowledge; handling delayed recurrence is new here.

repair.proposal: Before p29-q6-f, model: 0.0\dot{4} = (4/9) ÷ 10 = 4/90 = 2/45; then 0.1\dot{4} = 1/10 + 4/90 = 13/90. State that each additional decimal place before repetition divides the recurring contribution by another 10, and any whole-number part is kept separately. Add guided completion: 0.2\dot{7} = 2/10 + (7/9) ÷ 10 = ___; answer 5/18.

findings.doneWhen: Students see how to scale a recurring contribution and combine it with a non-repeating prefix before independent conversions.

findings.finding: The final ×100 annotation incorrectly describes the transition from 60/100 to 60%.
findings.breakdown: These representations are equal. Multiplying 60/100 by 100 gives 60, whereas 60% equals 0.6. The preceding arrows operate on numerator and denominator together, making the final annotation particularly misleading.
findings.checked: Calculated each transition: 9/15 = 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%. p32-q2-a correctly writes hundredths as a percentage, and p31-teaching-decimals confirms the percentage's value; neither makes the final multiplication annotation correct.
findings.assumptions: The annotations describe the adjacent transitions, consistently with the preceding arrows. Calculator availability is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Replace the final ×100 annotation with 'write hundredths as %', retaining 60/100 = 60%.

findings.doneWhen: Every annotation correctly describes its transition while preserving the represented value.

findings.finding: The score 28 out of 30 requires a recurring percentage beyond the demonstrated whole-number equivalent-hundredths method.
findings.breakdown: Simplifying to 14/15 does not yield denominator 100 through the whole-number operations modelled so far. The teaching has not connected fractional hundredths or division to an exact recurring percentage.
findings.checked: Reviewed p32-q2, p33-q3 and p34-q5: their conversions reach integer hundredths. p18-common-fdp provides the one-third benchmark but no general conversion route. The general conversion diagram appears later, in topic 9.
findings.assumptions: No general fraction-to-percentage method outside the supplied teaching is assumed. The gap concerns the conversion method, not calculator arithmetic.

repair.proposal: Before p35-q12, model: 'Equivalent hundredths can have a fractional numerator: 26/30 = (260/3)/100 = (86 2/3)/100 = 86 2/3% = 86.\dot{6}%. Here we multiply numerator and denominator by 10/3.'

findings.doneWhen: A fractional, recurring percentage is modelled before students convert 28 out of 30.

findings.finding: The first dissection moves sharply from counting supplied equal-area parts to constructing and combining area units.
findings.breakdown: Students must now choose helper subdivisions, distinguish unequal labelled regions from equal units, and combine or subtract areas before converting them. These decisions appear together without a bridge.
findings.checked: p41-q4 and p41-q5 supply equal-area partitions. Earlier visual conversion teaching does likewise. p41-q6 supplies comparisons rather than area decomposition. No preceding question bridges the decomposition demand.
findings.assumptions: Rectangle and triangle area reasoning is prior knowledge, consistent with the separate area booklets. Calculator use does not resolve the decomposition decision.

repair.proposal: Before the first dissection, add: 'Try extending existing boundaries to split regions into rectangles and triangles. A diagonal divides a rectangle into two equal-area triangles. Find a labelled region by combining these smaller areas or subtracting known areas from a larger region, then compare it with the whole square.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route into area decomposition while still determining each region's fraction and percentage themselves.

findings.finding: Classification requires rules for non-square integer roots and rational transformations of irrational numbers that the teaching does not supply.
findings.breakdown: The definitions and isolated examples do not give students a valid way to classify unfamiliar roots or expressions such as √5 + 1 and √2/2. The identification prompt correctly excludes treating a finite calculator display as proof.
findings.checked: p43-rational-vs-irrational names π and √2. p43-real-number-diagram-block gives particular examples. Earlier topics teach rational representations. p44-key-ideas restates decimal criteria without adding root or transformation rules.
findings.assumptions: These classification rules are new in this introductory irrational-number sequence. Calculator evaluation of roots is available but cannot establish irrationality.

repair.proposal: Before p44-identify, add: 'For a positive integer n, √n is rational if n is a perfect square and irrational otherwise. For example, √9 = 3 is rational; √5 is irrational. Adding a rational number to an irrational number, or multiplying or dividing an irrational number by a nonzero rational number, gives an irrational number. Thus √5 + 1, 2√2 and √2/2 are irrational. Use the original expressions to decide, rather than the calculator display.'

findings.doneWhen: The classification criteria are stated before unfamiliar roots and rational transformations are classified.

findings.finding: Generalise regrouping between whole units and fractional pieces while preserving a fixed value.
findings.breakdown: The task explains the existing p17-q12-e–h comparison and distinguishes regrouped sums from standard mixed numerals.
findings.checked: The rule-based conversions and the definition of a proper fractional part supply the required methods. For integer k from 0 to 5, 7k + (39 − 7k) = 39; only k = 5 leaves a proper fractional part.
findings.assumptions: An optional generalisation may use a letter to describe a whole-number choice.

repair.proposal: After p17-q12-h, offer: 'Starting with 39/7 = 5 + 4/7, explain how to reduce the whole part by one without changing the value. Write a sum using any whole-number part k from 0 to 5. Which is a standard mixed numeral?' Expected answer: removing a whole adds 7 to the numerator; 39/7 = k + (39 − 7k)/7. Only k = 5 gives the standard mixed numeral 5 4/7.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects the existing regrouping pattern to a general expression.

findings.finding: Use the recurring-block fraction pattern to find an exact complement to one.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects a two-digit recurring decimal with its numerator over 99.
findings.checked: 64/99 + 35/99 = 1, so the required decimal is 0.\overline{35}. The pattern is established within p28-q4, and the follow-up uses its existing value.
findings.assumptions: Subtracting fractions with a common denominator is prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: After p28-q4-fraction-c, add part j: 'What recurring decimal must be added to 0.\overline{64} to make exactly 1?' Answer: 0.\overline{35}, since 64/99 + 35/99 = 1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional next part asks for the exact recurring complement.

findings.finding: Compare π and 22/7 beyond the precision at which their rounded values agree.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison reinforces the difference between an approximation and an exact value.
findings.checked: To three decimal places, π ≈ 3.142 and 22/7 ≈ 3.143. Their difference is approximately 0.001264489, which rounds to 0.00126. Calculator approximation and rounding are already used in this topic.
findings.assumptions: Calculator access is explicit in p47-q8.

repair.proposal: After p47-q8-f, add: g. 'Round π and 22/7 to 3 decimal places.' Answers: 3.142 and 3.143. h. 'Find 22/7 − π to 5 decimal places.' Answer: 0.00126. i. 'Explain why their shared rounded value of 3.14 does not mean they are equal.' Answer: rounding hides their difference; more precise values differ.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up separates its three questions and retains the numerical comparison.

findings.finding: Compare one recurring fraction with successively closer terminating percentages.
findings.breakdown: The fraction stays fixed while terminating percentages approach it without becoming equal.
findings.checked: 30%, 33%, 33.3% and 33.33% are each less than 1/3. Also, 3/8 = 37.5% < 37.6%. Existing parts compare terminating and recurring values but do not provide this controlled run.
findings.assumptions: All conversions and comparisons are available by the end of topic 11.

repair.proposal: Append under the existing ascending-order instruction: 'Predict the order before converting.' m. 1/3, 30%; answer: 30% < 1/3. n. 1/3, 33%; answer: 33% < 1/3. o. 1/3, 33.3%; answer: 33.3% < 1/3. p. 1/3, 33.33%; answer: 33.33% < 1/3. Follow with unpatterned q. 3/8, 37.6%; answer: 3/8 < 37.6%. Only the terminating percentage varies in m–p.

findings.doneWhen: The run and unpatterned follow-up appear with only the single added prediction instruction.

findings.finding: Explain why repeating blocks of different lengths can describe the same decimal.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the denominator patterns with equivalent fractions and distinguish a repeating block from its shortest description.
findings.checked: The patterns over 9, 99 and 999 are established in p28-q3–q5. The equalities 4/9 = 44/99 = 444/999 and 23/99 = 2323/9999 are correct.
findings.assumptions: Equivalent-fraction arithmetic is available by the end of the topic.

repair.proposal: After p29-q6, offer: 'Predict whether 0.\dot{4}, 0.\overline{44} and 0.\overline{444} are equal. Convert each to a fraction to explain. Then give two repeating-block descriptions of 0.\overline{23} and explain their equality.' Expected answer: 4/9 = 44/99 = 444/999; for example, 0.\overline{23} = 0.\overline{2323}, since multiplying 23/99 by 101/101 gives 2323/9999.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain equivalent repeating-block descriptions using the taught fraction patterns.

findings.finding: Find which whole-number percentages correspond to an exact count out of 25.
findings.breakdown: Students generalise the equivalent-fraction structure already used to find counts from percentages.
findings.checked: p36-q16 supplies the denominator-change method and p36-q17 applies it to 25. For an integer percentage p between 0 and 100, the count is p/4, which is an integer exactly when p is divisible by 4.
findings.assumptions: The question concerns exact counts in a class of 25.

repair.proposal: After p36-q18-response, offer: 'A class has 25 students. Which whole-number percentages from 0% to 100% can describe an exact number of students? Explain using equivalent fractions.' Expected answer: 0%, 4%, 8%, …, 100%, because p/100 = (p/4)/25 and the count must be a whole number.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the multiples-of-four condition through equivalent fractions.

findings.finding: Compare a fixed recurring fraction with successively longer terminating approximations.
findings.breakdown: The run exposes why additional matching digits bring values closer without making a finite decimal equal to the recurring value.
findings.checked: Recurring notation and decimal ordering have been taught. Every listed terminating decimal is less than 2/3; the follow-up order is 66.6% < 2/3 < 0.667. No supplied run varies only the number of terminating sixes.
findings.assumptions: Students compare exact recurring values rather than rounded calculator displays.

repair.proposal: After p51-q1-h, add: 'Predict whether each value is smaller than, equal to or greater than 2/3. Insert <, = or >: 0.6 __ 2/3; 0.66 __ 2/3; 0.666 __ 2/3; 0.6666 __ 2/3. What changes, and why does equality never occur?' Answers: all <; the terminating string grows, but 2/3 has further sixes indefinitely. Keep 2/3 fixed and vary only the number of terminating sixes. Follow with: 'Order 0.667, 66.6%, 2/3 in ascending order.' Answer: 66.6%, 2/3, 0.667.

findings.doneWhen: The run includes prediction, explanation and an unpatterned comparison using the same distinction.

protectedGroups.observation: The same numerator can belong to a proper or improper fraction depending on the denominator.
Less than, equal to and greater than one are distinct cases; equality belongs within the improper category.
Moving the pointer changes the numerator while the whole-number component and denominator remain fixed.
protectedGroups.varies: Pointer position within the second whole.

protectedGroups.observation: One interval to the right increases the fractional component by one fifth.
protectedGroups.varies: Pointer position from the third to the fourth fifth after two.
protectedGroups.invariant: Fifth-unit scale and whole-number component two.

protectedGroups.observation: The same numerator can represent different whole counts and remainders when the fractional unit changes.
Different counts and sizes of fractional parts can regroup into the same number of complete wholes.
protectedGroups.invariant: Three wholes with no leftover parts

protectedGroups.observation: Each additional whole contributes five fifths, and this relationship extends beyond the displayed number line.
Counting fractional intervals still gives an improper fraction when intermediate numerical labels are removed.
protectedGroups.varies: Availability of intermediate labels, denominator and target value
protectedGroups.invariant: Conversion by counting equal fractional intervals from zero

protectedGroups.observation: Increasing the whole by one adds five fifths; increasing the fractional numerator by one adds one fifth.
protectedGroups.varies: Whole-number part in a–c, then fractional numerator in c–e.
protectedGroups.invariant: Denominator 5; numerator 1 in a–c, then whole-number part 3 in c–e.

protectedGroups.observation: The denominator determines how many fractional units each whole contributes.
protectedGroups.varies: Denominator in e–g, then whole-number part in g–h.
protectedGroups.invariant: Whole-number part 3 and fractional numerator 3 in e–g; denominator 9 and fractional numerator 3 in g–h.

protectedGroups.observation: Doubling the numerator doubles the represented quantity even when its mixed-number form changes.
Halving the denominator doubles the represented quantity and can produce whole-number results.
Trading one whole for seven sevenths preserves the total value.
protectedGroups.varies: Specified whole-number part decreases by one each time.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing an integer's sign does not prevent its representation with denominator 1.
Increasing the power-of-10 denominator moves the same numerator into smaller place-value positions.
The same numerator produces different decimal positions as the denominator changes.
Each tenfold decrease in decimal value requires a tenfold increase in denominator when the numerator stays fixed.
protectedGroups.varies: Decimal position and the missing denominator.

protectedGroups.observation: Unit-fraction values decrease as their positive denominators increase, regardless of whether their decimals terminate or recur.
A denominator of 6 can produce recurring decimals, a terminating decimal or a whole number; the numerator matters.
protectedGroups.invariant: Denominator 6 and the instruction to convert to a decimal.

protectedGroups.observation: Successive sevenths produce cyclic rearrangements of a six-digit repeating block.
The numerator of a proper fraction over 9 becomes its single recurring digit.
Fractions over 99 generate two-place recurring blocks, preserving a leading zero when necessary.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator and whether it occupies one or two digits.

protectedGroups.observation: Fractions over 999 generate three-place blocks, preserving leading zeroes.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator length from one to three digits.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the whole-number part and then delaying repetition have different effects on the fractional part.
protectedGroups.varies: First the whole-number part, then the position at which the same block begins repeating.
protectedGroups.invariant: Recurring block 43 and conversion to a fraction.

protectedGroups.observation: Equivalent fractions retain the same decimal value.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator and denominator are both multiplied by ten.

protectedGroups.observation: Multiplying the denominator by ten divides the recurring decimal value by ten.
The position of the fractional digit changes the place-value denominator.
protectedGroups.invariant: Whole-number part 6 and fractional nonzero digit 5.

protectedGroups.observation: The consecutive values 30%, 3% and 0.3% expose successive division by ten while percentage-to-decimal conversion remains division by 100.
The consecutive values 0.50, 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005 distinguish a redundant trailing zero from a change in place value.
Distinguishes two-digit percentages, removable trailing zeroes and necessary placeholder zeroes.
Equivalent fractions produce the same percentage.
The same scaling method works below and above one whole.
Terminating and recurring decimals are both rational despite their different decimal behaviour.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the digit 3 terminates or repeats.

protectedGroups.observation: Adding 1 changes the integer part without changing irrationality.
protectedGroups.invariant: Underlying irrational root and decimal tail.

protectedGroups.observation: Doubling √6 changes its location, while 2√6 and √24 coincide.
protectedGroups.varies: Multiplier and expression representing the number.
protectedGroups.invariant: Irrational classification; the final two rows also preserve value.
